meta.disclaimer: Market-level observations about participants in the Australian data-centre market, built from public data. Nothing here describes any lender's exposures or counterparties.

signals.title: Hyperscaler baseline: capex ÷ operating cash flow
signals.mechanism: When capex takes more of the anchor tenants' operating cash flow, less free cash stands behind their leases.
signals.headline: In their latest fiscal years, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Meta spent $465bn on capex against $635bn of operating cash flow (73%); the year before, $259bn against $489bn (53%).
signals.notes: Latest reported fiscal year each, ending 31 Dec 2025 (Amazon, Alphabet and Meta), 31 May 2026 (Oracle) and 30 Jun 2026 (Microsoft); the as-of is the newest year-end. In those years the five spent $464.6bn of capex against $634.9bn of operating cash flow, leaving $170.4bn of free cash flow. Their last four reported quarters of capex sum to $691.0bn; the inputs carry no quarterly operating cash flow, so the ratio stays annual. Capex here is cash purchases of property and equipment; assets taken on finance leases in the same fiscal years are outside it: $34.7bn for Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Meta (SEC XBRL, rou_additions.csv).
signals.cadence: ETL lane: quarterly capex, annual statements
signals.formula: Σ capex ÷ Σ operating cash flow across Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Meta, each at its latest reported fiscal year; the change is against each one's previous fiscal year. Per company: capex ÷ operating cash flow, FCF = operating cash flow − capex, net debt = total debt − cash and equivalents (negative = net cash), and capex summed over its last four reported quarters. Annual, not the latest quarter: the inputs carry no quarterly operating cash flow. Each fiscal year is dated by its year-end (the period of its annual capex row in quarterly_financials); the as-of is the newest of the five year-ends.
signals.chart: Latest fiscal year, per hyperscaler
signals.adverse_reason: A higher share of operating cash flow going to capex leaves less free cash behind the anchor tenants' leases.

signals.title: Hyperscaler leases signed but not yet commenced
signals.mechanism: Leases an anchor tenant has signed but not yet started are fixed payments that move onto its balance sheet as each one commences, ahead of the revenue the capacity is for; the faster they grow, the larger the claim on its future cash flow.
signals.headline: The five hyperscalers had $1,304bn of leases signed but not yet commenced on 30 Sep 2026, Microsoft the most at $365bn; $1,091bn on 30 Jun 2026.
signals.unit: US$bn signed, not yet commenced: five hyperscalers
signals.notes: Each company at its newest stated figure: Microsoft 30 Sep 2026; Amazon 30 Sep 2026; Alphabet 30 Sep 2026; Oracle 31 Aug 2026; Meta 30 Sep 2026. Undiscounted future payments as each lease note states them; scope differs by filer (each row's note in the table says how). Not commenced, so not yet on any balance sheet. Lease liabilities already booked for the five: $312.4bn (present value, SEC XBRL), a different measure: the two are never added. Meta: finance-lease liability not filed for the newest date, operating only. 5 venture and guarantee claims are listed in the table; several sit inside the not-yet-commenced totals or each other (each row says which), so none is summed. CoreWeave and Nebius are listed, not counted.
signals.owner: Curated file (quarterly Brain dashboard To-Do); lease liabilities: ETL lane
signals.cadence: Quarterly, curated from each 10-Q / 10-K lease note after the reporting season
signals.formula: Σ amount_usd_bn of each company's newest row in leases_not_commenced.csv on the date, for Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Meta: undiscounted future lease payments as each 10-Q or 10-K states them, each at its own balance date; as_of is the newest of the five. The series is the same sum at each calendar quarter end, where all five have a figure dated on or before it; the change is against the sum 3 months before as_of (else 1 month). Beside it, not added: operating + finance lease liabilities on each balance sheet (present value, SEC XBRL, lease_liabilities.csv), and venture and guarantee claims curated from the same filings, listed with what each overlaps. CoreWeave and Nebius are listed, not counted.
signals.chart: Signed, not yet commenced vs lease liabilities on the balance sheet, by company
signals.adverse_reason: More leases signed but not yet started is a larger fixed claim on the hyperscalers' future cash flow, ahead of the revenue the capacity is for.

signals.title: Compute commitments ÷ ARR, frontier labs
signals.mechanism: The more years of current revenue a lab's compute commitments represent, the more its leases, and any guarantee behind them, rest on growth and new funding; it moves as commitments are announced or ARR changes.
signals.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic have announced $1,013bn of compute commitments between them, against $135bn of ARR (7.5×); on 1 Jul 2026 the figures were $868bn and $72bn (12.1×).
signals.notes: OpenAI and Anthropic, the labs with both series: $1,013.2bn of announced compute commitments (OpenAI at 22 Jul 2026, Anthropic at 1 Oct 2026) against $135.0bn of ARR (OpenAI at 29 Sep 2026, Anthropic at 31 Jul 2026). Three months earlier, on 1 Jul 2026, the multiple was 12.1× (commitments: OpenAI at 27 Feb 2026, Anthropic at 20 Apr 2026; ARR: OpenAI at 1 Feb 2026, Anthropic at 31 May 2026). xAI ($20.0bn committed) and Mistral ($2.3bn committed) have no ARR series, so they are in the chart and table but not the sum. ARR is each lab's annualised run rate as it states it or as reported (the latest period's revenue scaled to a year): a point in time, not a forecast, not contracted, and not adjusted for churn. Commitments are announced cumulative totals, most over multi-year terms. The multiple therefore reads as years of current revenue the commitments represent; it is a constructed proxy, not a standard credit ratio.
signals.cadence: On announcement; monthly curation pass
signals.formula: Σ latest compute_commitments ÷ Σ latest arr, both USD bn from frontier_lab_valuations.csv, over the labs with both (of OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Mistral), each lab's latest row on or before the date. compute_commitments is the lab's announced cumulative total: deal values as announced, which mix take-or-pay minimums, ceilings and lease rent, so it is not a filed figure. Where a filing confirms a component, the row's notes cite it; a lab's total is restated only against a single company-stated aggregate, never rebuilt by adding filed categories (Anthropic's S-1 confirms one component, the Broadcom lease rent, and states no aggregate, so its total still includes the Fluidstack deal the filing does not state). as_of is the newest date among the rows the sum uses. Per lab: commitments, ARR, the date each was stated, and commitments ÷ ARR. The series and the change are over the same labs: the series from the first date they all had both, the change 3 months back where they all had both then, else 1 month, else since the previous observation.
signals.chart: Compute commitments and ARR per lab, and their ratio
signals.adverse_reason: More years of revenue committed to compute means the labs' leases rest more on growth and new funding.

signals.title: Funding cadence: lab raises ÷ ARR
signals.mechanism: A lab raising more often, or more against ARR, is funding burn; its lease then rests on the runway between rounds.
signals.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic raised $232bn in the 12 months to 22 Oct 2026, against $135bn of ARR (1.7×), plus $97bn of facilities signed but undrawn (2.4× with them); in the 12 months to 22 Jul 2026, $255bn against $72bn (3.5×).
signals.notes: OpenAI and Anthropic, the labs with an ARR series, raised and drew $232.4bn in the 12 months to 22 Oct 2026 against $135.0bn of ARR; facilities they signed in the window but have not drawn add $97.0bn (2.4× with them), outside the multiple. xAI ($20.0bn) and Mistral ($3.8bn) have no ARR series, so they are in the chart and table but not the multiple. The register begins 21 Jan 2025, so the multiple is drawn only for 12-month windows it covers in full; a round leaving the window moves it as much as a new one entering. Checked in the curation pass of 10 Nov 2026; newest deal 22 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass; the news catalogue carries the announcements
signals.formula: Σ USD bn raised and drawn in the 12 months to the register's newest deal (the as-of date: the newest date in funding_deals.csv) by the labs with an ARR series ÷ Σ their latest ARR on or before that date (frontier_lab_valuations.csv, metric arr). A raise is a funding_deals.csv row whose entity is OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI or Mistral AI itself and whose type is equity, debt, hybrid, debt_convertible, ipo or revolver; balance_sheet spending, acquisitions and vehicles a lab anchors (Stargate JV) are not its raises. Drawn = amount_bn − undrawn_bn (the register's optional column; blank means all drawn): an undrawn facility is not in the multiple, and the undrawn facilities signed in the window are shown beside it, in USD bn and as the multiple with them added. Per lab: months from the last raise to the as-of date, the gap before it, and raise ÷ ARR at the time (the latest ARR on or before the raise date; — where there is none). Stale after 90 days from the later of the newest deal and the last monthly curation pass (fetcher_log.json, monthly-curation-pass.last_run), which checks both registers whole.
signals.chart: Raises per frontier lab, marker area = USD bn; hollow markers are undrawn facilities
signals.adverse_reason: Raising more against revenue means a lab is funding more burn, so its lease rests on a shorter runway.

signals.title: Guarantor concentration: largest guarantor's share
signals.mechanism: The larger the share of lease obligations one guarantor backstops, the more the market's credit rests on one name whose fortunes depend on the same demand; it moves as guarantees are announced or run off.
signals.headline: NVIDIA backs $111bn of the $231bn of lease and compute guarantees in force on 29 Oct 2026, Broadcom $72bn and Google $48bn; on 29 Jul 2026 the largest was Google, with $43.8bn of $79.1bn.
signals.unit: % of guaranteed value in force: NVIDIA
signals.notes: 6 guarantees in force on 29 Oct 2026, $231.3bn from 3 guarantors; NVIDIA backs $111.3bn of it. Three months earlier, on 29 Jul 2026, the largest was Google at 55.4%. A guarantee counts as in force from its announcement date until its term runs out, and without end when no term is disclosed. 2 with no term disclosed ($47.2bn, 20% of the total) are counted as in force. Amounts are as announced, not amortised over the term. Checked in the curation pass of 10 Nov 2026; newest guarantee 29 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass, as the funding-deal register
signals.formula: Largest guarantor's share = Σ amount_usd_bn in force of the guarantor backing the most ÷ Σ amount_usd_bn of all guarantees in force, on the register's newest date (as_of, from the date column). In force: dated on or before the date and not past date + term_years; a row with no term_years counts as in force. Amounts as announced, not amortised. The series is the largest share at each quarter end and on as_of, whoever leads on each date; the change is against the largest share 3 months before (else 1 month, else at the previous announcement). With it: Σ in force by guarantor on every date that changes (each announcement, each term end), and Σ announced by guarantor in each quarter. Stale after 90 days from the later of the newest guarantee and the last monthly curation pass (fetcher_log.json, monthly-curation-pass.last_run), which checks the register whole.
signals.chart: Guaranteed value in force, by guarantor
signals.adverse_reason: A larger share behind one guarantor concentrates the market's credit in one name exposed to the same demand.

signals.title: Circular-financing share of tracked deals
signals.mechanism: When the funder is also the customer or guarantor, one balance sheet's stress propagates through the lease; it changes how much a guarantee is worth.
signals.headline: 24 of the 42 deals tracked in the 12 months to 22 Oct 2026 are circular (the funder is also the customer or guarantor), $440bn of their $635bn; in the 12 months to 22 Jul 2026, $483bn of $692bn.
signals.notes: 42 deals dated in the 12 months to 22 Oct 2026, 24 marked circular: $439.5bn of $634.7bn. A trailing window: a large deal leaving it moves the share as much as a new one entering. Checked in the curation pass of 10 Nov 2026; newest deal 22 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass; the news catalogue carries the announcements
signals.formula: Circular share = Σ amount_bn of deals marked is_circular ÷ Σ amount_bn of all tracked deals, over the 12 months to the newest deal. With it: Σ circular amount by entity and by quarter. Stale after 90 days from the later of the newest deal and the last monthly curation pass (fetcher_log.json, monthly-curation-pass.last_run), which checks the register whole.
signals.chart: Tracked deal value by quarter, circular and not
signals.adverse_reason: A larger circular share means more deals whose funder is also the customer or guarantor, so one balance sheet's stress travels further.

signals.title: Listed AU operator leverage
signals.mechanism: As listed AU operators' debt to equity rises, a smaller fall in lease income strains debt service.
signals.headline: Debt to equity is 24.4% at Goodman Group, 20.8% at Macquarie Technology and 55.3% at NEXTDC, from their latest balance sheets; Goodman's figure covers the whole group, mostly industrial property; the median was 36.4% as of 20 Apr 2026.
signals.unit: % debt to equity, median of 3 listed
signals.notes: The median of 3 ASX-listed operators' debt to equity (GMG, MAQ, NXT), each from its latest reported balance sheet, dated 2 Nov 2026 by the newest week of the price history. Balance sheets: the oldest is dated 30 Jun 2026; the reading is stale once it is over 253 days old. Net debt ÷ EBITDA and capex ÷ operating cash flow are not in the AU lane's files. Goodman's ratio is the whole group's, most of it industrial property. Earlier values are the quotes file as it stood on each date, from its recorded history (data/history/au_quotes, 10 versions since 13 Apr 2026), corrections included: a change can be a market move or a fix to the data. On 2 Aug 2026 it stood as recorded on 20 Apr 2026.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly quotes; ratios move with semi-annual statements
signals.formula: Median, across the listed operators, of debt to equity: total debt ÷ shareholders' equity, in %, from each one's latest reported balance sheet, as the AU lane's Yahoo Finance quotes carry it (NXT, GMG and MAQ at present; others as they list). Per operator with it: EV/EBITDA and market capitalisation. As of: the newest date in financials_history.parquet, written in the same run as the quotes, which carry no date, so it dates the prices: stale after 21 days. Also stale when the oldest operator's balance sheet (most_recent_quarter, the period end the ratio comes from) is over 253 days old: a half-year plus the ASX's two months to report it, plus a week. Net debt ÷ EBITDA and capex ÷ operating cash flow are not in these files, so they are not computed. Change: the same median of the quotes as they stood 3 months before as_of (else 1 month), from their recorded history.
signals.chart: Listed AU operators: leverage and valuation (share prices on Company Analysis)
signals.adverse_reason: Higher debt to equity means a smaller fall in lease income strains the operators' debt service.

signals.title: Open-weights share of the cost–capability frontier
signals.mechanism: When open-weights models hold more of the cost–capability frontier, capable tokens get cheaper and cheaper tokens get used, which moves inference volume and the data-centre space it needs.
signals.headline: Of the 13 models no rival beats on both price and GPQA score, 6 are open-weights, against 7 of 12 on 13 Aug 2026: since then 4 proprietary models and 1 open-weights model joined, and 4 dropped off.
signals.notes: 112 of the snapshot's 448 models carry a GPQA score and both prices; on 13 Nov 2026, 13 sit on the frontier, 6 of them open-weights. Each quarter's frontier is rebuilt from the models released by its end at the snapshot's current prices, so a later price cut moves earlier quarters too; 7 models with an unknown licence are left out of the share and counted (0 of them on the frontier). At GPQA ≥ 75% the cheapest proprietary model, Mercury 3 at $0.163 per 1M tokens, costs 2.3× the cheapest open-weights one, GPT OSS 120B at $0.070. The snapshot was fetched on 13 Nov 2026; its newest model release is dated 11 Nov 2026. The change compares with today's leaderboard limited to the models released by 13 Aug 2026, at today's prices: no version in today's format was recorded by then.
signals.cadence: ETL lane: ZeroEval leaderboard pull, every one to three weeks
signals.formula: Frontier = data_llm.pareto_front over blended price ((3 × input_price + output_price) ÷ 4, USD per 1M tokens) and GPQA, of the models released up to a date that carry a GPQA score and both prices; a model priced the same as a more capable one is not a member. Open share = members whose licence is neither proprietary nor unknown ÷ members of known licence (unknown left out and counted), at the snapshot's own date (_meta.updated, the fetch date and the as-of) and at each quarter end. Also stale when the snapshot's newest model release is over 60 days old (a stalled upstream, however recent the fetch). The change is against the frontier of the leaderboard as it stood three months earlier, from its recorded history, else of today's models released by then. Cost gap = cheapest proprietary ÷ cheapest open-weights blended price among models at GPQA ≥ 75% (cheapest_frontier's threshold).
signals.chart: Price against GPQA with the frontier, its open-weights share by quarter, and the cost gap
signals.adverse_reason: A larger open-weights share makes tokens cheaper, which can bring more inference volume and more leased space, but it also squeezes the frontier labs' margins as tenants.

signals.title: Cheapest price for fixed capability (GPQA ≥ 75%)
signals.mechanism: The rate at which the price of a fixed unit of capability falls is the rate at which a tenant's revenue per token falls, so its return on leased capacity depends on volume outrunning it.
signals.headline: GPT OSS 120B, at $0.070 per M tokens since 5 Aug 2025, is still the cheapest model scoring at least 75% on GPQA; at 85% and above, first reached at $3.44 in Nov 2025, the cheapest is now $0.113.
signals.unit: per M tokens, cheapest at GPQA ≥ 75%; 0.0% year on year
signals.notes: Cheapest at ≥ 75% GPQA on 13 Nov 2026: $0.070/MTok (GPT OSS 120B, released 5 Aug 2025); a year earlier $0.070, three months earlier $0.070, so 0.0% year on year and 0.0% over 3 months. No new low in the last 3 months. At GPQA ≥ 85%: $0.113/MTok (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Max, released 23 Apr 2026), from $3.44 when a model first reached it (GPT-5.1 Instant, 12 Nov 2025). Each model is at its price in this snapshot and dated by release, so the line is rebuilt at every pull; the 2020–25 launch prices carry no capability score and are context only. The change's earlier price is rebuilt from today's file (models released by 13 Aug 2026, at today's prices): no version in today's format was recorded by then. The snapshot was fetched on 13 Nov 2026; its newest model release is dated 11 Nov 2026.
signals.cadence: ETL lane: ZeroEval leaderboard pull, every one to three weeks
signals.formula: P(t) = the cheapest blended price, (3 × input + output) ÷ 4 in $ per million tokens as data_llm.preprocess_ze blends it, among leaderboard models scoring at least 75% on GPQA and released by t (data_llm.cheapest_frontier's running minimum, each model at its snapshot price). Value = P(as of). Change = 100 × (P(as of) ÷ P(3 months earlier) − 1), the price's % change (1 month when there was no price 3 months earlier), P(3 months earlier) from the leaderboard as it stood then when its recorded history holds a version in today's format; year on year the same, rebuilt from today's file, over 12 months. Beside it, the same price at GPQA ≥ 85%, where the 75% price has stopped falling. As of = the leaderboard's _meta.updated, its fetch date; also stale when the snapshot's newest model release is over 60 days old. The 2020–25 launch prices, blended the same way, carry no capability score: context on the chart only.
signals.chart: Cheapest $/MTok at GPQA ≥ 75% and ≥ 85%, log scale, against 2020–25 launch prices
signals.adverse_reason: A falling price for the same capability cuts a tenant's revenue per token, but cheaper tokens can also bring more inference volume and more leased space.

signals.mechanism: A hyperscaler keeps renewing in Australia while its AI capex pays back; when capex outruns its cloud revenue and the backlog contracted behind it, the case for each renewal option weakens.
signals.headline: Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle spent $587bn on capex from Q4 2025 to Q3 2026, 112% of their $522bn of cloud revenue, against 101% for Q3 2025 to Q2 2026.

signals.notes: Σ capex $586.6bn ÷ Σ cloud revenue $522.1bn across Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle, 2025Q4 to 2026Q3, the newest quarter with capex and cloud revenue for all of them. Capex is as v_hyperscaler_capex records it, each company's cash purchases of property and equipment: assets taken on finance leases are not in it, and it is the whole company's, not its AI capex alone. Cloud revenue is the line the file's notes name (a segment, or Microsoft Cloud revenue, a metric across Microsoft's segments), so the ratio is a proxy for payback, not a return; Meta has no cloud revenue in the file and is in the table only. Microsoft's cloud revenue is its Microsoft Cloud revenue (Azure, Microsoft 365 commercial cloud and Industry solutions cloud) in every quarter: Microsoft has reported no Intelligent Cloud segment since 2026Q3, and published Microsoft Cloud revenue for the quarters before on the same basis. Assets taken on finance leases over the same quarters, outside the capex: $28.8bn for Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet (SEC XBRL, rou_additions.csv); not filed for all four quarters by Oracle. RPO / backlog is as each company reports it, so its scope differs: Microsoft's commercial RPO, Amazon's AWS backlog, Alphabet's Google Cloud portion of $567.7bn remaining performance obligations and Oracle's RPO. A few large contracts with frontier labs can make up much of a backlog; T1 (compute commitments, Frontier labs) carries them. Tokens, as the file's notes give them: Alphabet 2026Q3, “First-party model APIs: nearly 32bn tokens/minute (press release; the earlier rows said Gemini API) = 46.1T/day; x30.44 days = ~1,403T/month, an upper bound since the release says nearly”.
signals.cadence: Quarterly, after earnings; the curation job updates the disclosures
signals.formula: Capex ÷ cloud revenue = Σ capex (v_hyperscaler_capex) ÷ Σ cloud_revenue (ai_demand_disclosures.csv) over the four calendar quarters to the newest quarter that every hyperscaler with cloud revenue in the file has disclosed, %; the change is on the quarter before. Per ticker, at its newest disclosed quarter: capex ÷ cloud revenue; RPO or backlog ÷ capex over the four quarters to it; the disclosed AI run-rate and tokens processed (where given). A fiscal quarter counts in the calendar quarter in which it ends. A window is summed only when Microsoft's rows in it name one line: it has reported no Intelligent Cloud segment since 2026Q3, so its quarters are to be its Microsoft Cloud revenue, and a window whose rows name more than one line is not summed. No aggregate consumer AI spend is shown: it is not observable from disclosures. as_of = the newest capex period end (v_hyperscaler_capex.period) the value uses.
signals.chart: Capex, cloud revenue and RPO by quarter, per hyperscaler; tokens processed where disclosed
signals.adverse_reason: Capex running further ahead of cloud revenue means the AI spend is paying back more slowly, which weakens the case for each renewal.

signals.title: Hardware density trajectory vs tier-1 facility envelope
signals.mechanism: An option in 2040 is exercised only if the shell can house 2040's hardware; this moves when vendors' rack power and cooling needs outrun the design envelope a tier-1 operator builds to today.
signals.headline: NVIDIA's newest rack, Rubin Ultra NVL576, due in 2027, is stated at 600 kW, as is CDC Data Centres' liquid-cooled design envelope; a trend fitted to all 4 racks since 2018 reaches 600 kW in late 2028.
signals.unit: years until the fitted trend passes 600 kW per rack

envelope.document: CDC update, Infratil Investor Day, ASX filing of 18 Sep 2025 (p. 131)
envelope.quote: CDC's cooling technologies enable cutting edge +600 kW high-density and high floor loading for advanced compute workloads.

signals.notes: The table's 4 NVIDIA rack configurations (2018–2027), fitted log-linear, grow 37% a year; the fitted trend reaches the envelope in 2028.9, and the newest row, Rubin Ultra NVL576 (Kyber rack) (2027), is stated at 600 kW per rack. The envelope, 600 kW per rack with liquid cooling, is the stated design capability of CDC Data Centres (CDC update, Infratil Investor Day, ASX filing of 18 Sep 2025 (p. 131), linked in the table: “CDC's cooling technologies enable cutting edge +600 kW high-density and high floor loading for advanced compute workloads.”), never any facility's fit-out; AirTrunk publishes no kW figure and NEXTDC's own pages disagree. One table edit so far, so no earlier value; perf per watt is on GPU Hardware & Pricing, and AMD has no row because it states no rack-level power.
signals.cadence: On vendor roadmap events; the table is edited by hand
signals.formula: Fit ln(rack kW) = a + b × year by least squares over the table's rows (one per accelerator generation: the densest rack configuration the vendor publishes; year = the availability year the vendor stated at announcement, placed at mid-year). Crossing year t* = (ln E − a) ÷ b, E = the tier-1 envelope in kW per rack. Value = t* − as_of, in years: positive is the headroom left at the fitted rate; zero or negative means the fitted trend passed the envelope that many years earlier (shown negative, never floored at zero). Change = value now − value at the previous table edit, each from the table as it stood at that edit. as_of = the date of the newest edit.
signals.chart: Rack power by generation against the tier-1 envelope
signals.adverse_reason: Fewer years before the density trend passes today's design envelope means more of today's shells will not house the hardware of their option dates.

signals.title: Hyperscaler AU capital announced
signals.mechanism: Hyperscalers' stated capital and sites for Australia run ahead of their leasing; this moves when they announce, and a slowdown here would precede fewer new leases and less certain renewals.
signals.headline: Microsoft (A$30bn) and Amazon (A$20bn) have announced A$50bn for Australia since 24 Oct 2023; the 4 announcements since 14 Jun 2025, from 4 companies, added A$25bn.
signals.notes: 6 announcements dated 24 Oct 2023 to 28 Sep 2026, 3 with an A$ figure (A$50.0bn in all; 4 announced since 14 Jun 2025, to 28 Sep 2026, adding A$25.0bn); the figures are multi-year statements of intent, some capital and operating spend together, not contracted leases. 10 site leads (tier A 5, tier B 3, tier C 2) carry no date, so they show a level, not a change. The project database has no hyperscaler flag, so the MW counted in it are those of the projects an announcement links, 550 MW in all: NEXTDC S7, 550 MW facility (Proposed), linked 05 Dec 2025.
signals.owner: AU lane (seeds from the AI & DC curation job)
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the manual seeds
signals.formula: Announced capital = Σ capex_aud_m ÷ 1,000 over every announcement dated on or before the newest announcement_date, in A$bn (an announcement with no figure is counted but adds nothing). Change = the last step in the sum: the capital the newest announcement with a figure added, measured from the announcement with a figure before it (the previous watermark, and the date the row's change runs from); a register that has only one figure falls back to the capital newly announced in the 3 months to the date, else 1 month. With it: the cumulative sum at each quarter end, by company; site leads counted by evidence_tier (the lead register has no date, so a level, never a change); and linked MW = facility_mw in projects.parquet of each project an announcement's linked_project names (matched on project_name, and on operator = linked_operator where a name repeats). as_of = the newest announcement_date.
signals.chart: Announced AU capital by quarter, cumulative; site leads by evidence tier
signals.adverse_reason: Slower announced capital can mean weaker demand, but it can also mean supply discipline, or political and council limits that favour incumbents already holding land, so it cuts both ways and is not counted.

signals.title: Demand growth needed to fill the risked pipeline
signals.mechanism: Renewals are negotiated against spare capacity when filling what can actually be built needs faster demand growth than the published scenarios; this moves when projects advance or drop out, or the scenarios are revised.
signals.headline: Electricity use by data centres on the NEM needs to grow 29% a year (26% on 13 Aug 2026), from 4.0 TWh in 2025 to 24.0 TWh in 2032, to run today's fleet and the risk-weighted pipeline at a mature 50% use; published scenarios grow 15–29%.
signals.notes: NEM regions: 37 operating projects record 1,640 MW (25 more disclose no MW and add nothing); the pipeline to 2032 is 2,700 MW risked of 12,777 MW unrisked; the pipeline outside the NEM (WA, 200 MW risked) shows only by region. full_capacity_year is recorded for 1 of 45 NEM pipeline projects, so 17 are placed by startup_year and 27 undated ones (711 MW risked) at 2032; as AEMO notes new facilities take five to ten years to reach a mature rate, the comparison is made at 2032, not year by year. PUE 1.32 is the median of the 48 NEM projects with MW that state one; at AEMO's 45–51% the needed growth is 27.3–29.6% a year, and on the 2025 actual the operating stock runs at 21% (AEMO: 27% of connection capacity in quarter 1 2026). Earlier values are the project database as it stood on each date, from its recorded history (data/history/au_projects, 19 versions since 13 Apr 2026), corrections included: a change can be a market move or a fix to the data. On 13 Aug 2026 it stood as recorded on 5 Jul 2026. The scenarios are today's file. Since these projects were last checked, the news catalogue has headlines naming their operator with a word such as withdraw, cancel or delay: NEXTDC, 10 projects (1 item, 21 Oct 2026: “Australian AI data centre operator NextDC shares shed 42% on revenue delay, future plans on hold”, Reuters). 87 of 117 projects (97% of the MW) were checked in the last 120 days; half the MW was last checked on 7 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: Needed growth = (D ÷ A)^(1 ÷ (H − Y)) − 1, in % a year. A = the latest actual NEM data-centre consumption (TWh in Y, the last Baseline year of dc_demand_forecasts.csv); H = the last year all three scenarios reach; D = the TWh that would run the operating stock plus the pipeline dated by H at a mature utilisation: D = Σ MW × k × u × 8,760 ÷ 10^6, over NEM regions (NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1, TAS1). MW = risked_mw (the project database's existing risk weights; risk_base_mw for the unrisked case); k = PUE for MW recorded as IT load or a campus envelope, 1 for MW recorded as facility power (capacity_basis power_consumption_mw, gross_power_mw, grid_connection_mva). u = 50%: AEMO's mature-fleet utilisation of connection capacity (AEMO, 2026 ESOO (Aug 2026), p. 36: 45–51% by data-centre type, around 50% in aggregate; 45% and 51% are shown too: https://www.aemo.com.au/-/media/files/electricity/nem/planning_and_forecasting/nem_esoo/2026/2026-electricity-statement-of-opportunities.pdf?rev=4f2e73fbd906456288198fdbc24b335a&sc_lang=en). PUE = the median pue of the NEM projects with MW that state one (value and count in the notes). A pipeline project (any status but Operating) is placed at its full_capacity_year, else startup_year, else H, and no earlier than Y + 1; one dated after H is left out. Each scenario: growth = (its TWh in H ÷ A)^(1 ÷ (H − Y)) − 1, and utilisation = its TWh ÷ the TWh of the stock plus pipeline at full use. The scenarios are national, so regions are a breakdown, not compared one by one; the regional ESOO supply surplus is not used, as its maximum demand already includes AEMO's own data-centre forecast. as_of = the newest last_verified_at in projects.parquet. Also stale when half the risked-base MW was last checked over 120 days ago (the MW-weighted median last_verified_at). Change: the same needed growth, against the same scenarios, from the database as it stood 3 months before as_of (else 1 month), from its recorded history; series: at each month end.
signals.chart: Demand needed at mature use vs the scenarios (NEM, TWh); MW by region
signals.adverse_reason: Needing faster demand growth to fill what can be built means more spare capacity when renewals are negotiated.

signals.title: Pre-commitment ratio: share of capacity contracted
signals.mechanism: Capacity built against signed contracts carries renewal risk, and capacity built on spec lease-up risk first; this moves when operators sign contracts or add capacity, and a falling share is an early sign of oversupply.
signals.headline: CDC Data Centres is the only one of 11 operators to disclose both contracted and total capacity: 1,100 MW of its 4,180 MW across Australia and New Zealand is contracted (26%), as of 6 Oct 2026.

operators.geography: Global portfolio with Sydney project line

beyond_australia.geography: Global portfolio with Sydney project line

breakdown.chart_note: Left off the chart and the totals, as it is not an Australian figure: Goodman Group's 6,400 MW of capacity, stated for “Global portfolio with Sydney project line” (20 Aug 2026).
breakdown.chart_dates: figures dated 10 Sep 2025 to 6 Oct 2026; 1 undated (Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners)

signals.notes: Contracted 1,100 MW against 4,180 MW of capacity for the one operator disclosing both, CDC Data Centres (capacity stated 06 Oct 2026, contracted 06 Oct 2026): each operator's latest figure of each kind, paired. It states 42.4% of the 9,867 MW of Australian capacity in the seed (7 of 11 operators give a figure); NEXTDC's contracted 740 MW has no capacity figure here. Left out, as stated for a geography wider than Australia: Goodman Group's 6,400 MW of capacity. No like-for-like change: the basis of the capacity figures changed since the previous point (05 May 2026, 34.4%), CDC Data Centres's from built capacity pipeline to leasable capacity pipeline.
signals.owner: AI & DC curation job (seed); AU lane rebuilds
signals.cadence: Semi-annual: operator results and valuations
signals.formula: Per operator: contracted_capacity_mw ÷ (operating_capacity_mw + under_construction_mw + future_build_mw), a blank part counted as 0, or ÷ total_capacity_mw where the row gives no breakdown; each operator's latest dated contracted figure is paired with its latest dated capacity figure. Market figure = Σ contracted ÷ Σ capacity over the operators with both, in %. Disclosing share = their capacity ÷ the capacity the file states across all its operators (each operator's latest figure). as_of = the newest announcement_date among the rows the market figure uses. The change is since the previous point, over the same operators. A row stated for a global, worldwide or international geography is left out of all of it: it is not an Australian figure.
signals.chart: Contracted and stated capacity, by operator
signals.adverse_reason: A falling contracted share means more capacity is being built on spec, the early sign of oversupply.

signals.title: Power-secured share of announced pipeline
signals.mechanism: Only pipeline with secured power can become supply competing with leased sites at renewal; this moves as announced projects secure power, and a low share means announced competition is softer than its headline MW.
signals.headline: Of the 10,400 MW in 33 proposed or approved projects, 3% (314 MW) has power recorded as secured, 51% as not secured and 46% has no record either way; on 13 Aug 2026 the database recorded 5% as secured.
signals.unit: % of Proposed + Approved MW; 46% not recorded
signals.notes: 33 Proposed or Approved projects stating 10,400 MW: 314 MW (3.0%) with power recorded as secured, 5,275 MW (50.7%) recorded as not secured and 4,811 MW (46.3%) with no record either way, so the secured share would be 49.3% if every unrecorded project had power. MW is each project's stated capacity (facility_mw), which mixes IT load and site power envelopes, campus full-build figures included, as the sources give them. The date is the newest last_verified_at among these projects. Earlier values are the project database as it stood on each date, from its recorded history (data/history/au_projects, 19 versions since 13 Apr 2026), corrections included: a change can be a market move or a fix to the data. On 13 Aug 2026 it stood as recorded on 5 Jul 2026. Since these projects were last checked, the news catalogue has headlines naming their operator with a word such as withdraw, cancel or delay: NEXTDC, 3 projects (1 item, 21 Oct 2026: “Australian AI data centre operator NextDC shares shed 42% on revenue delay, future plans on hold”, Reuters). 30 of 33 projects (99% of the MW) were checked in the last 120 days; half the MW was last checked on 16 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: Secured share = Σ MW of Proposed and Approved projects with power_secured = true ÷ Σ MW of all Proposed and Approved projects, national, in %. MW per project = facility_mw (the database's stated capacity), else critical_it_mw, else it_load_mw; a project with none is counted as without a figure and adds no MW. power_secured empty (not recorded) is neither true nor false: its MW stays in the denominator and is shown beside the share, with the share if all of it were secured. By region: secured, not secured and not recorded MW per nem_region. as_of = the newest last_verified_at of those projects. Also stale when half their MW was last checked over 120 days ago (the MW-weighted median last_verified_at). Change: the same share of the database as it stood 3 months before as_of (else 1 month), from its recorded history; series: at each month end.
signals.chart: Proposed and Approved MW by region, by power status

other_sign.note: the first place limits on new grid connections show

signals.adverse_reason: A higher secured share means more of the announced pipeline can become supply that competes with leased sites.

signals.title: AI-workload share of the AU pipeline
signals.mechanism: The more capacity is built for AI, the more its renewals rest on AI inference economics; this moves as AI campuses are announced or start operating, and sizes how far the renewal signals reach.
signals.headline: Of the 13,237 MW in 47 proposed, approved or under-construction projects, 44% (5,851 MW) is recorded as AI/HPC or mixed cloud/AI, against 0.2% (3 MW) of the 1,672 MW operating; on 13 Aug 2026 the pipeline's AI share was 80%.
signals.notes: Pipeline (Proposed, Approved and Under Construction): 47 projects stating 13,237 MW, 5,851 MW of it (44.2%) AI/HPC or Cloud/AI, of which Cloud/AI, a mix of AI and cloud, is 493 MW. Operating stock: 70 projects, 41 of them stating 1,672 MW, 3 MW of it (0.2%) AI; the other 29 state no MW, counted and adding nothing, so the operating share covers only the projects with a figure. MW is each project's stated capacity (facility_mw), which mixes IT load and site power envelopes, campus full-build figures included; 17 projects record no workload type (5,838 MW), shown as a class of its own. The date is the newest last_verified_at. Earlier values are the project database as it stood on each date, from its recorded history (data/history/au_projects, 19 versions since 13 Apr 2026), corrections included: a change can be a market move or a fix to the data. On 13 Aug 2026 it stood as recorded on 5 Jul 2026. Since these projects were last checked, the news catalogue has headlines naming their operator with a word such as withdraw, cancel or delay: NEXTDC, 10 projects (1 item, 21 Oct 2026: “Australian AI data centre operator NextDC shares shed 42% on revenue delay, future plans on hold”, Reuters). 87 of 117 projects (97% of the MW) were checked in the last 120 days; half the MW was last checked on 7 Oct 2026.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: AI share = Σ MW of pipeline projects whose workload_type is AI/HPC or Cloud/AI ÷ Σ MW of all pipeline projects, in %; pipeline = every status but Operating (Proposed, Approved, Under Construction). Beside it, the same share of operating stock (status Operating). Cloud/AI mixes AI and cloud workloads and is counted as AI, shown on its own in the table. A project with no workload_type is its own class (not recorded), never Traditional, and is not AI. MW per project = facility_mw (the database's stated capacity), else critical_it_mw, else it_load_mw, as S3; a project with none is counted as without a figure and adds no MW. By region: MW per workload class per nem_region, operating and pipeline. as_of = the newest last_verified_at. Also stale when half the MW was last checked over 120 days ago (the MW-weighted median last_verified_at). Change: the same share of the database as it stood 3 months before as_of (else 1 month), from its recorded history; series: at each month end.
signals.chart: Workload mix of operating and pipeline MW, by region
signals.adverse_reason: A higher AI share means more demand behind the build but also more capacity whose renewals rest on AI economics, so it sizes the other signals rather than leaning one way.

signals.title: Grid-connection queue (US proxy)
signals.mechanism: The longer a new data centre waits to energise, the longer incumbents with connected power hold their pricing at renewal; a shorter queue or wait means competing supply arrives sooner.
signals.headline: US grid-connection queues held 2,061 GW of generation and storage in 2025 (Berkeley Lab, published 1 May 2026), down from 2,290 GW for 2024 (published 15 Dec 2025). The median wait from request to operation was 5.0 years.

avg_wait_time_years.source: Rand et al. (2024) UChicago/LBNL queue analysis [DERIVED]
Rand et al. (2024) UChicago/LBNL queue analysis [DERIVED]

signals.notes: US queue depth for 2025 is 2,061 GW (LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition, published 01 May 2026), 229 GW less than for 2024; the newest US Avg Wait Time is 5.0 years (2025). LBNL reports the wait from connection request to commercial operation as a median for a build cohort, and each edition's cohort differs, so a change between editions mixes cohort and method. LBNL counts generation and storage seeking a US grid connection, not data-centre load: a proxy for connection friction. The AU queue is S4-AU, beside it on this dossier.
signals.cadence: Annual: LBNL Queued Up edition (the curation job updates the file)
signals.formula: Queue depth = the United States 'Queue Depth' row (GW of generation and storage seeking a grid connection, LBNL Queued Up) for the newest year in dc_queue_metrics.csv, read from the newest edition where a later one restates the year. Change = that minus the previous year's figure, since the previous year's published_date. Beside it: the United States 'Avg Wait Time' rows (years from connection request to commercial operation; the spec's 'median time-to-COD', the file's name kept). ERCOT and PJM Interconnect rows are listed in the table, not charted: single-market figures from other sources, not comparable with the national series. as_of = the published_date of the queue-depth row the value uses.
signals.chart: US queue depth (GW) and Avg Wait Time (years), by year
signals.adverse_reason: The US queue is mostly generation and storage, so a shorter or faster queue brings power sooner to sites that would compete with leased ones, adding supply, while a deeper queue means longer waits that protect incumbents already holding connected power.

signals.mechanism: The longer a new data centre waits for a grid connection in Australia, the longer incumbents with connected power hold their pricing at renewal; a shorter queue means competing supply arrives sooner.

Beside it: each region's queue depth and median_days_to_connect (median days from application to connection, AEMO NEM Connections Scorecard), charted for NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1 and TAS1; other rows, such as the NEM total, are tabled. signals.title: Delivered power price, NSW1
signals.mechanism: Power is passed through to the tenant, so a rising delivered price lowers the tenant's return on the site and is the lever it pulls at renewal.
signals.headline: NSW1's wholesale price averaged A$74.5/MWh in the year to 30 Sep 2026, down from A$78.4/MWh in the year to 30 Jun 2026. Q3 2026 averaged A$74.3/MWh, against A$90.0/MWh in Q3 2025.
signals.notes: NSW1, 365 days of prices in the 12 months to 30 Sep 2026: wholesale A$74.5/MWh; no network row is in force for NSW1, so this is wholesale alone. A rolling year, so the winter peak does not read as a change; each region's latest full quarter against the same quarter a year earlier is in the table.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly NEMOSIS pull of AEMO's monthly archives
signals.formula: Delivered price = wholesale (AEMO regional reference price, RRP) + the network charge in force (AER, where published), A$/MWh. Each region's rows are averaged by calendar day first; a network row applies from its date until the region's next one. Headline: NSW1, the mean daily delivered price over the 12 months to the newest price date; change = that minus the same 12-month average three months earlier. Beside it: quarterly averages by region, wholesale and network stacked, and each region's latest full quarter against the same quarter a year earlier (YoY). as_of = the newest NSW1 wholesale date.
signals.chart: Quarterly price by NEM region: wholesale, with the network charge stacked where published
signals.adverse_reason: A higher delivered power price lowers the tenant's return on the site and is the lever it pulls at renewal.

signals.title: Regulatory changes reaching existing assets
signals.mechanism: This moves when a regulator or government applies a network charge, levy, operating obligation or planning condition to data centres already built, which raises the cost of running them under leases already signed.
signals.headline: 2 of the 10 instruments dated in the 12 months to 2 Oct 2026 apply to existing facilities or connections: NSW DCCEEW's consultation paper (17 Aug 2026) and AEMC's (24 Sep 2026); on 2 Jul 2026 none did.
signals.unit: of 10 items in 12 months reach existing assets

items.instrument: Improving the NEM access standards – Package 2 (ERC0394): draft rule determination
items.summary: Draft rule sets a tiered framework for applying access standards to large loads, with new disturbance ride-through and instability standards for large inverter-based loads such as data centres.

items.instrument: Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers
items.summary: Five national expectations, including that new data centres secure new clean energy to offset their demand and cover their share of network costs; Commonwealth assessments prioritise the proposals most closely aligned.

items.instrument: Powercor distribution determination 2026–31, Attachment 16 (connection policy): final decision
items.summary: Load customers newly connecting at 22 kV or above, which includes most data centres, pay the tax on their type 1 capital contributions upfront.

items.instrument: AI in Australia's interests: Australian Standards for AI (announcement)
items.summary: Announces standards, expected to be legislated in early 2027, under which large data centres would underwrite their own new power supply, pay their full share of connection costs and reduce power when needed.

items.instrument: Operational integration and visibility of large inverter-based loads (ERC0455): rule change request
items.summary: Asks the AEMC for rules on operational visibility, monitoring, communication and information sharing for large inverter-based loads such as data centres.

items.instrument: Data centre energy obligation: advice to Energy and Climate Change Ministers
items.summary: Recommends that data centres offset their consumption with certificates from new renewable generation, contract for firming capacity and meet market registration requirements, with demand flexibility supported through connection agreements.

items.instrument: Reforming electricity network connection and cost recovery arrangements for data centres in NSW: consultation paper
items.summary: Ten proposed reforms for data centres of 15 MW or more, including an entry bond, a Major Network Upgrade Fee, contributions to jurisdictional scheme costs from transmission-connected data centres and information obligations on proposed and existing connections.

items.instrument: NSW Data Centre Policy Framework and NSW Data Centre Guidelines
items.summary: Six principles for data centre projects, including investment in additional water and energy supply; projects that meet the performance measures are assessed within 75 days.
Would require new data centres to bring their own renewable supply and storage, meet connection and network upgrade costs, cool with recycled or non-drinking water and keep 150 metres from homes.

items.instrument: Cost recovery for network augmentations – Packages 1 & 2 (ERC0448, ERC0456): consultation paper
items.summary: Consults on the Minister's requests that data centres and other large loads pay the network costs they cause, including prudential requirements, transmission-level recovery of jurisdictional scheme costs and a public register of large loads.

signals.notes: 10 items in the register, 10 of them dated in the 12 months to 2 Oct 2026, its last review: 2 that apply to existing facilities or connections as their sources state, 5 to new developments or connections only and 3 whose sources say neither. Items include proposals, consultations and announcements as well as made rules; the instrument column gives each one's stage. 2 such items are dated after 2 Jul 2026. The register was last reviewed on 2 Oct 2026, after its newest item (24 Sep 2026), so it is dated by that review.
signals.cadence: On event; monthly curation pass
signals.formula: Count = items in regulatory_register.csv with affects_existing = yes, dated in the 12 months to as_of (as_of − 365 days < date ≤ as_of). affects_existing is what each item's source says: yes where it says the instrument applies to existing facilities or connections, no where it says new or expanded developments or new connections only, unclear where it says neither. as_of = the later of the register's newest item date and its last review (fetcher_log.json, regulatory_register.last_run; the newest item alone when that record is missing or unreadable). Change = the count at as_of less the count three months earlier (one month when the register does not reach back three). Series: the count at each quarter end and at as_of. Chart: one mark per item by date, in a lane per affects_existing reading (categorical colours, unclear in grey), with the 12-month window shaded.
signals.chart: Regulatory instruments by date, by whether they apply to existing assets
signals.adverse_reason: More rules reaching existing assets raise the cost of running sites under leases already signed.
